https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9kg.text: Image source, News1 Image caption, Surveillance footage show a group of masked men spraying lacquer across the restaurant in South Korea's Seongnam By Kelly Ng Published 30 September 2026, 05:21 BST A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say. Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer. The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent". The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported. The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said. "People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent." In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues. The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; Â£8,400). Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery. Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province. Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition. Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars. https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/uk-news/po.text: NATO members are preparing plans for evacuating their populations in the event of an attack by Russia , according to reports. The plans focus around an area called the Suwałki Gap which connects the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad with the Russian-allied state of Belarus via a 60-mile stretch of the Polish and Lithuanian border. If Putin were to move his forces from Belarus across the gap to Kaliningrad, it would mean Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania could be cut off from the rest of Europe. Lithuania and Poland are currently working together on a framework for plans in case of Kremlin hostilities. The Lithuanian National Crisis Management Centre has announced the creation of a bilateral agreement alongside nationwide drills in the country which included plans for evacuation along the Polish-Lithuanian border. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre, explained plans will provide for the evacuation of Lithuania as well as Latvia and Estonia if necessary. He said: “Procedures, logistics, and infrastructure capabilities are being analysed together with colleagues from Poland, and the plan itself should be developed once an agreement is reached between the two countries.” Plans for a possible Russian invasion include border controls to “prevent people in certain key roles from leaving the country”. Some 3,000 officials and around 1,000 volunteers are taking part in the drills in Lithuania, along with around 20 Polish officials who have travelled there to take part. Earlier this month Polish prime minister Donald Tusk warned Russia was preparing drone and missile strikes against countries that had been supporting Ukraine . Donald Tusk issued the warning in the Polish parliament on last week, citing intelligence assessments which said Russia could carry out attacks against his country and other countries on NATO's eastern flank while presenting them as accidents. He said such attacks could be intended to test NATO's willingness to invoke Article 5, which requires member states to come to the aid of an ally under attack. His words came just days before after Poland was forced to scramble fighter jets on Wednesday after a Russian military helicopter crossed into its airspace . The Mi-8 made a brief incursion near the Polish town of Braniewo after entering the country’s airspace from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, the Polish military said. NATO jets were again scrambled over the country last Saturday (September 19) after Russia launched a wave of jet-powered drone strikes across neighbouring Ukraine.

Photograph: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP/Getty Images SpaceX SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas Uwa Ede-Osifo Fri 13 Nov 2026 19.53 EST First published on Fri 13 Nov 2026 18.38 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short. Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas . The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 Raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top. As smoke plumes wafted from the launch site, SpaceX employees erupted into cheers. SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The cause of that diversion remains unknown. “That certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” said Kate Tice, SpaceX’s director of quality management, but she noted the booster’s return was in line with “rigorous safety checks”. Early in the webcast, SpaceX simulated the return. The entire rocket was expected to be grabbed in the launch tower’s “chopstick” mechanical arms. Friday’s test did not rise to the double-catch mantle, which Elon Musk had described early in November as a “critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary”. Still, the flight is still poised to mark another milestone for the company. If all goes to plan, it would be the first time SpaceX has caught the rocket’s 171ft upper stage. Previous tests focused on the retrieval of the booster. The Starship, meanwhile, has continued to sail through space at over 26,000 km/h at an altitude of 270km. The launch went on as scheduled despite a nationwide ground stop that disrupted hundreds of flights. Flights to the west coast from Hawaii were temporarily paused, then resumed on Friday due to space debris from the launch, according to the island’s transportation agency. As in the past, Starship carried satellites for Starlink, SpaceX’s internet service wing, three of which were fitted with cameras to analyze the rocket’s heat shield. The data plays a role in determining if the spacecraft is ready to return. SpaceX chief executive Musk has sought to advance Starship’s “rapid reusability” as a vehicle, which he hopes will take humans to the moon and, controversially, to Mars. Nasa has contracted SpaceX, along with Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to provide the lunar landers that will return astronauts to the moon in 2028. Musk has cast his reusable rocket as a buffer against the enormous costs associated with future space travel. SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights in recent years, some of which have resulted in explosions that signaled major design flaws. In September, the most recent flight test, SpaceX notched a victory, sending the spacecraft into Earth’s orbit for the first time , although its engine failed during the ascent.
